title: Chapter 75 – Forty Steps
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Mountain Gate Trial begins at dawn on the day of the new moon, and the whole Outer Court comes to watch.

They line the bottom of the Hundred Stairs in ranks, gray tunics on the left, brown on the right, a few white-robed inner disciples standing apart on the Contribution Hall's steps with their hands in their sleeves. Four hundred people, perhaps. The air is cold and clear and smells of snow that has not yet arrived. Overhead, the stair rises into the morning haze, a pale ribbon of stone that climbs the mountain in twelve long flights and vanishes into cloud.

Jian stands in the third rank of the first-years with Ma Bao on one side and Pei on the other.

"It is not a race," Ma Bao is saying, for the fourth time. He is a broad cheerful boy with a cut on his chin and a talent for repeating what he has heard. "It is a measure. The array pushes down, you push up, the keepers write the number. Forty is junior. Sixty is named. My cousin reached fifty-two."

"What happens at eighty?"

"The Elders write your name in a book." Ma Bao says it with reverence. "Feng reached seventy-three. Nobody has reached eighty in nine years."

"What happens if you fall?"

"You do not fall." Ma Bao looks vaguely offended. "The array lets go. You slide down to the last landing you passed. It hurts, they say, like being a rug."

Jian says nothing. He has been awake since the third watch.

There is a table at the base of the stair, long and low, covered in black cloth, and at it sit the keepers: four elderly men in gray with brushes and tablets. The oldest, a stooped bald man with a face like a dried apple, is Keeper Fu. Jian has heard Feng speak of him. He sits very straight, with his tablet balanced on one knee, and his eyes do not wander over the crowd. They are fixed on the first step.

Behind them, on a raised platform under an awning, sit three Elders. Shen Wuye in his white robe, looking at nothing. Elder Bai in his plum-stained green, eating something from a paper twist. And between them, in iron-gray, with his heavy arms folded and his jaw set, Elder Duan of the Enforcement Hall.

He watches the first-years, thinks Jian. He watches Ma Bao and Pei and the silent boy. He watches me.

A gong sounds, once.

"First-years," calls a keeper's thin voice. "Outer Sect Disciples of the Spring Register. By number. Step forward when your number is read."

* * *

It goes slowly.

The first-years climb in groups of five, each boy and girl on a white flagstone before the first step, and the array wakes under them with a low, steady hum. It is a pressure array, the oldest kind. The deeper a disciple's cultivation, the harder it pushes. A breath after they step onto the first stair, the five bend slightly at the knees. By the tenth step they are gasping. By the twentieth, the group has strung out along the flight like beads on a loose cord.

Jian watches from the third rank and counts.

Pei, twenty-two. A girl from the south, twenty-nine. A tall boy with a torn sleeve, thirty-six, and a cheer from his courtyard. Ma Bao, thirty-one. The keepers write each number on their tablets, with a quick dry scratch. Ma Bao comes down the stair on a stretcher's arm, grinning, bruised across the shins, reeling.

"Thirty-one," he says, to everyone, to no one. "It pushed me flat."

"Lin Jian," calls the keeper. "Outer Sect 0417."

He walks to the white flagstone.

Four hundred people look at him. He feels it as a pressure of its own, like warm air. He is the smallest first-year by a hand. He wears the same gray tunic as the rest, a little too short at the wrists, and his sandals have been patched twice. He stands before the first step with his hands at his sides and the Seasons Veil turning false and slow beneath his ribs.

A boy of the third layer.

A voice in the crowd, not loud, says, "That is Feng's brother." Another says, "The Pill Hall one." And a third, quite distinct, from the white-robed ranks on the Contribution Hall steps: "They say he reads fire."

He puts one foot on the first stair.

The array wakes.

* * *

It is not pain. It is weight.

A hand the size of the sky settles on his shoulders and begins, patiently, to press. He has felt this before. He felt it in the Garden, the night the Seal formed, and in the Orchard, when the whole mountain leaned on him. But this is not the leaning of a living thing. It is mechanical, even, calibrated to the width of a hair. It does not hate him. It simply measures how much of him there is.

Ten.

He climbs. The stone is cold through his sandals. Behind him, the crowd's murmur falls away. Ahead, the flights rise one above another in the haze, each marked with a post of white jade at the landing. He keeps his eyes on his feet and lets his breath settle, in and out, with the slow wheel under his ribs turning the same false cycle it always does.

Twenty.

Here, he knows, a third-layer boy would be gasping. Jian lets his breath shorten, a little, by design. He rounds his shoulders. He lets his knees bend. He is an actor, and the audience is four hundred, and the part is a child who is doing quite well.

It is much harder than the climb.

Thirty. His shoulders ache, but not from the array. They ache from the lie. The Five Seasons Seal sits below his navel like a fist, quiet, patient, and under the pressure he can feel it begin to answer. It wants to push back. It is made for pushing back. Every ounce the array leans on him, the Seal leans a little harder against it, and the real Wheel under the false one begins to turn faster, and the Veil, which was made to hide a ninth-layer cultivator from a nose, must now hide one from a mountain.

He holds it. He counts. He breathes.

Thirty-five.

A bead of green light slips from his left wrist.

It is a thing the size of a seed. It rises along the inside of his sleeve and winks, once, against the cloth, in the exact color of new leaves. The Seal has pushed a breath of true Qi through a seam in the false wheel, and for the length of a heartbeat the Veil has a hole in it.

He stops dead on the thirty-fifth step. He folds his right hand over his left wrist, as if from cramp, and bends over it. A flight below him, a keeper lifts his head.

Slow. Let it go down.

He does not fight the Seal. That is the lesson of the Garden, and he learns it again in his shoulders: what is pushed will push back, and what is let flow will find its own level. He turns his attention inward, to the pale gold ring below his navel, and instead of clamping he opens, a hair, and lets the pressure bleed off through his feet into the stone. The green light dies. The Veil closes.

When he straightens, the keeper has looked away. A woman in the crowd is fanning herself. Nobody has moved.

His heart is going like a drum. He climbs.

There is a sound ahead, a faint high hum, like a finger drawn around the rim of a glass. He has heard it before. He heard it in a dream, in the Garden, on the night he found the cradle.

The fortieth landing.

* * *

It comes into view at the top of the fourth flight, out of the haze.

It is a wide stone platform, thirty paces square, with a post of white jade at each corner and a low parapet along the open side. Behind the parapet the mountain falls away in a long gray slope to the roofs of the Court. In front of the platform the stair resumes, narrower and steeper, rising toward the cloud. At the center of the platform stands a single post taller than the rest, with a white disk set into its face at the height of a man's chest.

It is the marker. All the first-years who reach forty put their palm to it, and a keeper below sees the number change. It is where the junior trial ends.

Jian puts one foot on the landing.

The pressure drops.

It is a sudden mercy, like stepping out of a river. The array thins here, as if exhausted, and his shoulders spring up half a hand. He breathes. The cold air burns in his chest. Below, a long way below, the crowd is a field of small gray dots, and a tiny voice floats up to him: "Forty!" It is not true. He is on thirty-eight. But the keepers below have a reading, and the reading says, he supposes, what it says.

He walks to the marker.

Palm on the disk. Then down. That is the plan. He will lay his palm on the white stone, and let the array tell the keepers what it likes, and walk back down the stair at the pace of a tired boy. He has decided it a dozen times in the dark.

He lays his hand on the post.

It is warm.

Not the warmth of stone in the sun. This is warmer, deeper, a slow steady glow, as of a thing breathing in its sleep. A thin line of light runs from the disk down the post, across the paving, and under his feet. And he sees it: not with his eyes, but with the other thing, the quiet inner sight that came with the Level 3 passive and has never yet failed him.

Seam-sight. No cost. No panel. The world, for a heartbeat, comes apart along its joints.

The platform is not a platform.

It is a lid. Under the polished stone, three paces beneath his feet, a vast pale lattice of Qi runs in rings about the post, thicker than the array above it, older, colder. It spirals inward, tighter and tighter, to a point directly beneath the disk. And at that point, in the heart of the stone, set into a cavity as neat as a socket in a joint, lies a thing he knows.

A plate. Round. Seven lobes.

It is the collar from the Garden. It is the same shape, drawn on a different scale, and it is not a collar here but a dock, with a hollow at its center the size and shape of a coil of silver wire.

The cradle.

He feels it in his sleeve, in the small gray pouch he took from Ke Tian's dead belt, where the cradle lies wrapped in oiled cloth against his hip. It does not hum. It does not glow. It simply, very faintly, leans, as a plant leans toward a window.

The post is warm against his palm.

The lock. It is not a lock to keep things out. It is a lock designed to be opened from here, at this stair, by this key, at this hour. He knows it with a certainty so complete that it frightens him. It was built for what he carries. And the landing, the forty steps, the junior trial, the pressure array, all of it is a lid on top of a mechanism six hundred years old, and every disciple of the Outer Court who has touched this post has put his hand on the top of a door without knowing it.

Now? he thinks, wildly. Here? With four hundred watching?

No.

He takes his hand away.

The warmth fades. The lines of light fade. The world closes along its seams like a book. He is a small boy on a stone landing in the cold, with a hand that tingles, and his heart is going like a hammer.

* * *

"You did not touch the marker."

The voice is dry, and very near.

He has not heard him approach. The old man has come up the stair behind him, silently, with a tablet on his arm and a brush tucked behind his ear. Keeper Fu stands with his stooped back to the long drop and his eyes, which are pale, wet and sharp as a bird's, fixed on Jian's face.

"I did, Keeper," says Jian. "I put my hand on it."

"You put your hand on it for a long time." The old man's voice carries no accusation. "You stood. You did not breathe. The disk is supposed to read in one breath." He lifts the tablet and consults it. "It read a very peculiar thing."

Jian waits.

"Forty," says Keeper Fu, "is what it read, at the first breath. Forty is what it should read. Forty is the end of the junior trial and the end of my duty." He turns the tablet toward the light. "And then it read forty-one. And then forty-two. And then the post stopped, and I had to climb up to see why."

Two extra.

"I do not understand, Keeper."

"Nor do I." The old man's eyes do not leave him. "The array measures how hard a disciple pushes. It does not measure how hard a disciple stands. Forty-one is a number the array reads from a person who has gone past forty, who has begun to take the next stair. You did not take the next stair. You did not move."

"Perhaps the array is old."

"Perhaps." The pale eyes are steady. "It has not been wrong in four hundred years. I would be much obliged to know what you were doing."

This is the moment, thinks Jian. This is the cost.

He has to give the old man something. Not a truth. Something that sits close enough to the truth to be believed, and far enough from it to be harmless. He looks at the post, at the disk, at the tablet. He lets his shoulders slump. He lets a little of the third-layer boy slip, and a little of the twenty-year-old appear in its place.

"I was tired, Keeper," he says. "I thought if I took my hand away, the number would go down."

For a moment nothing moves.

Then, to his surprise, the old man laughs. It is a dry, creaking, startled sound, like a gate.

"Tired." He wipes his eye with a thumb. "Forty years I have kept this stair, and I have been told a great many things by a great many boys, and no one has ever told me he was tired." He pats the tablet. "I shall write thirty-eight. It is a good number. It is a number for a boy who did well and is honest enough to say he is tired."

"Thank you, Keeper."

"I shall also write down the other number," says Fu, "in the book I do not show to anyone. I would like you to know that. It is my habit. It is why I have kept the stair so long." He looks at Jian, gravely. "When a thing happens at this post that the array cannot explain, I write it. In case it is explained later."

"Yes, Keeper."

"Go down."

He goes. He walks back down the long stair at the pace of a tired boy, with his shoulders rounded and his hands loose, through the weakening pressure and the cold bright air, and the crowd cheers at the bottom, not loudly, as for a boy who has done well and no better. Ma Bao thumps him on the back. Pei says, "Thirty-eight!" in a tone of awe. Across the dais, beneath the awning, Elder Bai eats a plum and looks out over the heads of the Court with perfect calm.

Elder Duan is looking at the stair.

His heavy arms are still folded. His eyes, which are small and flat and gray as lead, are fixed on the fortieth landing, high in the haze, and on the small stooped figure of Keeper Fu who is coming down the stair after Jian with his tablet in his hand and a frown on his dry face.

He knows the number was wrong, thinks Jian. He was not looking at me. He was looking at the post.

* * *

The results are read at noon, from the Contribution Hall steps, in the voice of a clerk who has done this many times.

"First-years of the Spring Register. Highest numbers." He unrolls a strip. "Tan Ruyan, Outer Sect 0031. Sixty-one."

A hush, and then a ripple of applause. She stands in the front rank of the gray tunics with her hands folded and her comb flashing, and receives it with the exact small bow of someone who expected a higher figure. Sixty-one is a named number. Her name will be cut on the stone beside the stair. A few of the white-robed inner disciples glance at her, and one of them, a young man with a jade pin, nods.

"Zhao Yao, Outer Sect 0112. Forty-nine."

The applause is thinner. Jian looks for him. The boy from Red Ridge stands at the end of the third rank, alone, in a gray tunic that is clean and plain and mended at the elbow, with a straight back and a set, pale, careful face. He is fourteen. He does not look at anyone. He looks at the stone of the stair, as if it were a thing he meant to remember.

Forty-nine. Better than any boy from the south. Worse, Jian suspects, than he could have done.

"Lin Jian, Outer Sect 0417. Thirty-eight."

There is a murmur, and a little laughter, kind and a little surprised. Someone says the Pill Hall one in a tone that settles the matter. Ma Bao thumps him again, harder. On the dais, Elder Bai licks a finger and does not look up.

And in the white-robed rank, behind the pillar, someone does not laugh.

It is the young man with the jade pin. He is tall, twenty perhaps, with a long calm face and heavy-lidded eyes. He is studying Jian the way a man studies a bridge he has been told is safe. He sees Jian see him. He does not look away. After a moment he inclines his head, the width of a thumb, in the manner of one honest merchant to another, and turns to say something to the man beside him.

He knows the number was a lie.

Or he knows it was only a number. Jian does not know which is worse.

* * *

Mo Lian watches the trial from the Contribution Hall's balcony.

Jian does not see him there at first. The Deacon stands at the back of the gallery in the shadow of a pillar, with his hands folded and his eyes lowered, as he has stood at the great scale on every working day of the year. His gray hair is combed flat. His robe is clean. He is attended by two clerks, who hold between them the great black register, as though it had weight. He watches the climb. He watches the numbers read.

When the clerk reaches the name Lin Jian, the Deacon looks up.

It is a long look across forty paces of cold bright air, over four hundred heads, between two pillars. He does not smile. He does not frown. His face is the face of a man looking at a ledger that has just balanced.

Then he turns his hand over, slowly, on the balcony rail, and shows the palm.

It is clean. There is nothing on it. It is perfectly dry and perfectly white.

He has washed it. Jian stands in the third rank with the sun on the back of his neck and understands the message as clearly as if it had been spoken. He wishes me to know there is nothing to see. That I imagined the glass.

It is a challenge, or a courtesy, or both. He does not respond.

Beside the Deacon, one of the clerks has leaned forward to whisper in his ear. Mo Lian listens, nods once, and lowers his hand.

The clerk straightens. He is a young man with ink on his cuffs and an expression of harried goodwill, and Jian has seen him before: it was he who stood at his elbow at the register. Now he is looking not at Jian but toward the stair, at the crowd, with a faint tight frown, as though trying to find someone in it.

He is looking for the pot.

Jian turns away. He does not know if the note has been found. He does not know if the pine on Terrace Nine has been visited. He knows only that before the third watch tonight he must be wherever he would be if he were afraid, which is in bed, and that when the third watch comes, whatever the Deacon does, it will happen without him.

* * *

The seedling sits in a clay pot on the stone beneath the old pine on Terrace Nine, and it is, as far as Jian can tell, a pine.

It is not a seedling of the Garden. It is a seedling of the hillside, a hand high and unremarkable, that he dug out of the shale behind the Pill Hall at dusk with a trowel borrowed from Han's boys. He has potted it in black soil. He has tied a loop of red thread round the stem. Pinned to the thread, in a small cramped hand, is a slip.

The Garden is held in trust by the Court. Apply to the Court.

It is not much of an answer. It is not, he thinks, the answer of a wise man. It is the answer of a boy who has run out of better ones. But he has weighed every possible reply to the note, as he weighs all things, and every one that gave something away led to the same end. A seedling of the Garden is a key. A seedling of the hill is a message.

I do not trade it. And I am not afraid to say so in writing.

He sets the pot down at the foot of the tree, in the fold of a root, where it will be found.

Then he walks away. He does not look back.

The new moon is a black hole in the sky. The stars are very close. He goes down the terrace steps by feel, and through the gate, and across the empty yard, with the weight of the day sitting heavy on him: the post, the plate, the two extra numbers, the old man's pale eyes, the warm stone. The thing under the landing is real. It is exactly where Feng said. It will open, if he wants it to, and he has not decided.

I have not decided, he thinks. I should decide soon.

He lies down on his cot in Reed Courtyard in the dark, with the pouch at his hip. Ma Bao is snoring. Pei is silent. Lan Tong is awake, he thinks; he can feel the boy's gaze across the room, patient as a cat's. He closes his eyes.

He does not sleep.

At the third watch, in the black center of the night, something moves in his pouch.

It is not a sound. It is not a light. It is a vibration, thin and delicate and long, that passes through the cloth and the oiled wrapping and the silver wire inside, and through his hip into the bone. It is a single note, very low, held for the length of one breath. It is exactly the note he heard at the post that morning.

It is answering.

Far above, a mountain's height away, in the cold dark on the fortieth landing, a seven-lobed plate hums once, and the cradle against Jian's hip hums back.
